title: Mirabel and the Visitor
premise: Orsen Blackwood returns to his family's decaying house in the village of Hollowmere to record its dying folk songs, only to find the imaginary friend of his childhood—Mirabel—waiting on the porch, unchanged after thirty years. As he documents the village's forbidden counting-song, he realizes the song is a tally: every verse sung marks a soul the Visitor will collect, and Mirabel has been keeping Orsen invisible from the count since childhood. When Orsen discovers that his own recordings have been feeding the count instead of preserving against it, he must choose between destroying his life's archive and letting the Visitor finish what it started. In the end, Orsen burns the recordings and sings the final verse himself, taking his family out ahead of the count—but Mirabel, revealed as the first collected child of Hollowmere, stays behind to hold the door shut, and Orsen leaves knowing loyalty cost him the only truth he ever loved.
about_author: Gideon Blackwood is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing oral histories in remote English villages before turning to fiction. He writes horror about the things we preserve too well.

chapters.title: The House That Remembers
chapters.summary: Orsen Blackwood arrives at Hollowmere with recording equipment and a scholar's detachment, moving into the abandoned family house. His POV establishes his compulsive documentation habit and estrangement from his sister Wren. The emotional beat is uneasy homecoming: the house feels expectant, as if it kept his room ready.

chapters.title: Songs They Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Orsen interviews elderly villagers about local ballads; each refuses to repeat the counting-song after one verse, going pale or leaving mid-sentence. His POV. The beat is scholarly frustration curdling into unease as he notices everyone counts their fingers before closing their doors.

chapters.title: Someone on the Porch
chapters.summary: At dusk Orsen finds a small figure on the porch swing: Mirabel, his childhood imaginary friend, exactly as she was at seven years old. His POV. The beat is vertiginous joy collapsing into dread when he realizes she hasn't aged—and doesn't know she should have.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: Orsen calls his sister Wren, urging her to visit with her daughter Ida; he can't explain why over the phone. Alternating POV with Wren, who remembers no 'Mirabel' and worries Orsen is unraveling again like after their mother's death. The beat is sibling friction masking love.

chapters.title: What Imaginary Friends Do
chapters.summary: Mirabel reenters Orsen's routines seamlessly—fetching things, humming harmonies, standing watch at night. His POV. The beat is seductive comfort; he catches himself talking to her aloud and feels more sane with her than without, which frightens him more than her existence.

chapters.title: The Verse Beneath the Verse
chapters.summary: Orsen records blind organist Tam Yew singing the counting-song's full eleven verses once, hands shaking. Analyzing the tape, he finds an undertone—a second voice under Tam's—that matches no villager alive. His POV. The beat is the thrill of discovery shadowed by the sense of being permitted to hear it.

chapters.title: Ida Counts to Eleven
chapters.summary: Wren arrives with six-year-old Ida, who immediately sees Mirabel and plays with her happily. Wren's POV, alarmed by her daughter's new friend and Orsen's calm acceptance. The beat is maternal terror: Ida starts skipping while chanting numbers she was never taught.

chapters.title: The Tally Explained
chapters.summary: Tam Yew, drunk and terrified, tells Orsen the truth: the song is a census for the Visitor, and each complete singing delivers a name. The village stopped singing it whole generations ago, but something has been singing it alone in the fens. His POV via recorded interview. The beat is revelation as curse—knowledge arrives too late to be innocent.

chapters.title: Invisible
chapters.summary: Mirabel confesses her purpose: she made Orsen uncountable as a child, hiding him inside herself, and she has held the hiding for thirty years alone. His POV. The beat is devastating tenderness—he understands at last why he always felt half-real, borrowed, deferred.

chapters.title: The Archive Problem
chapters.summary: Orsen reviews his field recordings and finds the Visitor's undertone has crept into every tape, growing louder with each session; his documentation has been broadcasting Hollowmere's names. His POV. The beat is the corruption of vocation—the prayer of preservation turned into an invitation.

chapters.title: First Loss
chapters.summary: Tam Yew is found at his organ, dead, fingers worn to the bone on the keys, having played the song through in his sleep. Orsen's POV. The beat is grief weaponized into guilt: the last tape Tam made sits labeled in Orsen's own case.

chapters.title: Get Out Ahead of the Count
chapters.summary: Orsen begs Wren to leave with Ida tonight; Wren refuses to abandon him, forcing him to reveal Mirabel—which Wren cannot see, hearing only her brother talking to air. Wren's POV. The beat is the loyalty/truth fracture: believing him means admitting the world is worse than she thought.

chapters.title: The Fen at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Orsen follows the undertone's source into the fen and finds a drowned chapel where generations of counted villagers stand preserved in peat, faces upturned, mouths open mid-verse. His POV. The beat is awe curdled into horror—he photographs everything before he can stop himself.

chapters.title: Mirabel's Name
chapters.summary: In the chapel's ledger Orsen finds the count began with a girl named Mirabel Blackwood, first collected in 1891, a relative erased from family memory. His POV. The beat is identity upheaval: his oldest friend is his family's oldest wound, and her loyalty may be a leash.

chapters.title: Confrontation on the Porch
chapters.summary: Orsen demands Mirabel release him from her protection so he can act freely; she refuses, and for the first time her face goes wrong—too many years pressed behind a child's shape. His POV. The beat is power's corruption surfacing: even love, hoarded thirty years, becomes possession.

chapters.title: Ida Is Counted
chapters.summary: Ida completes the song at her skip-rope game, all eleven verses, taught by a voice in the well water. Wren's POV, frantic. The beat is pure dread: Ida's name enters the count, and the Visitor's attention turns toward the house like weather.

chapters.title: Bargaining with the Doorkeeper
chapters.summary: Orsen offers the Visitor his archive—every recording, every documented name—in exchange for striking Ida from the count. The negotiation happens through Mirabel, who translates between them weeping. His POV. The beat is sacrifice offered and refused: the Visitor wants singers, not paper.

chapters.title: Burning the Prayer
chapters.summary: Orsen destroys his life's work—tapes, notebooks, the fen photographs—in the chapel fire, unmaking his documentation-as-prayer. Mirabel helps him, her hands passing through the flames untouched. His POV. The beat is terrible liberation: without the archive he is finally, fully real, and fully unprotected.

chapters.title: The Eleventh Verse
chapters.summary: The Visitor comes for the house. Orsen sings the counting-song himself, complete, inserting his own name as the eleventh verse to overwrite Ida's. Mirabel holds the threshold, her form stretching across the doorway. His POV. The beat is climax: loyalty enacted as self-offering, truth spoken in the enemy's language.

chapters.title: What Mirabel Was For
chapters.summary: The substitution works but cannot hold; Mirabel takes Orsen's place in the count, revealing she was always meant to be returned, not kept. She releases thirty years of hiding in one look. His POV. The beat is heartbreak transfigured—she chose him twice, and now chooses the children of Hollowmere instead.

chapters.title: Out Ahead
chapters.summary: Orsen, Wren, and Ida drive out of Hollowmere at dawn as the village's remaining elders, freed by the broken count, begin openly singing the song for the first time in living memory—as farewell, not summons. Wren's POV. The beat is exhausted relief shadowed by loss; Ida waves at someone in the rear window until the trees close.

chapters.title: Documentation
chapters.summary: A year later, Orsen keeps a single notebook containing one sentence: 'She was real.' He teaches folklore now, telling students some songs are doors and some are locks, and never says which this story is. Final pages shift between his POV and a last image of the porch swing moving in wind with no visitor. The beat is quiet, earned grief—truth survived, loyalty honored, identity chosen at last.
